This notebook contains the full code with intermediate data checks behind the poster *Examining the Link Between APC-Paying Institutions and Author Position* presented at the 2026 Conference of the Barcelona Declaration on Open Research Information. The poster itself presents a condensed selection of the findings below.

## Background

For paid open access, the dominant model is that article processing charges (APCs) are invoiced to the institution of the corresponding author [@Schimmer2015]. However, corresponding-author data has often been unavailable as open research information [@Jahn2026]. Some studies therefore used first author affiliation data as a proxy, for example, to identify articles published under transformative agreements [@Jahn2026;@Doerner2026]. This notebook tests the policy assumption against real payment data. To this end, the OpenAPC dataset for German institutions (regular APC payments and payments in the context of transformative agreements) is combined with author-level metadata from OpenAlex.

## Questions

To test the assumptions we consider the following questions:

- How complete is the coverage of OpenAlex corresponding-author data?
- How well does ROR-based matching work?
- At which author-position is the paying institution recorded as affiliation? 
- Are first and/or author affiliations a good proxy for identifying the paying institution?


## Data

The OpenAPC dataset in version v5.11.5-5-1 [@OpenAPC2026] was used to collect APC data for German institutions. Specifically, we restricted the OpenAPC dataset to the files `apc_de.csv` (which contains journal article APC payment data), `transformative_agreements.csv` (which contains APC payment data in the context of transformative agreements), and `institutions.csv` (which links institution names from the other files to Research Organization Registry (ROR) IDs). 

To retrieve OpenAlex author-level metadata, the OpenAlex Walden snapshot from 2026-06-26 was used. Data were accessed through the SUB Göttingen [Open Scholarly Data warehouse](https://console.cloud.google.com/bigquery?hl=en&project=subugoe-collaborative) on Google BigQuery.

The Research Organization Registry (ROR) data set in version v2.11 [@ROR2026] was used to collect ROR IDs and institutional relationships for German institutions.

The code for combining the OpenAPC data files, filtering the OpenAPC data for German institutions and the publication period 2021--2025, and querying Google BigQuery is available in the `bigquery.R` script in the data folder.

## Data preparation

The OpenAPC data was previously filtered for German institutions and the publication period 2021--2025. The analysis is conducted with the following R objects:

- `apc_df` (OpenAPC): one row per APC payment. Important columns: `doi`, `ror_id` and `institution_full_name` (the *paying* institution), `period` (publication year), `publisher`, `agreement` (filled for transformative agreements).
- `oal` (OpenAlex): one row per author-affiliation combination for all articles in the OpenAPC dataset, 2021--2025. Important columns: `doi`, `author_position` (first, middle, last), `is_corresponding`, `author_id`, and the affiliation of the author (`ror`, `institution_display_name`). An author with two affiliations appears in two rows.
- `ror`: one row per institution. Important columns: `id` (ROR ID) and `relationships` (parent, child, related institutions).


```{r}
glimpse(apc_df)
```

```{r}
glimpse(oal)
```

```{r}
glimpse(ror)
```

### Normalization

1. `oal_all`: DOIs and ROR IDs in the OpenAlex data are converted to lower case to prevent mismatches in case of any capitalisation differences. `oal` is deliberately **not** filtered by country to keep all authors of an article, otherwise foreign first or corresponding authors would be excluded and distort the positions.
2. `ror_de`: only German institutions from the ROR dataset are kept, together with their relationships. They are needed for matching the paying institutions, which are all German, via relationships. ROR IDs are converted to lower case to prevent any mismatches in case of capitalisation differences.
3. `apc_joined`: Rows without DOI are dropped (without DOI there is no link to OpenAlex) within the OpenAPC dataset. The DOI in OpenAPC has no `https://doi.org/` prefix, so it is added before joining. DOIs and ROR IDs are converted to lower case to prevent mismatches in case of capitalisation differences. Then the OpenAlex data is joined via DOI (`inner_join`: only articles found in both sources remain), and the ROR data of the *paying* institutions is joined via ROR IDs (`left_join`: no paying institution is lost if it is missing in `ror_de`).


```{r}
oal_all <- oal |>
  mutate(
    doi_norm   = tolower(doi),
    ror_author = tolower(ror)
  )

ror_de <- ror |>
  filter(locations.geonames_details.country_code == "DE") |>
  select(id, names.types.ror_display, names.types.label, relationships) |>
  mutate(id = tolower(id))

apc_joined <- apc_df |>
  filter(!is.na(doi)) |>
  mutate(
    doi_norm = tolower(paste0("https://doi.org/", doi)),
    ror_norm = tolower(ror_id)
  ) |>
  inner_join(oal_all, by = "doi_norm") |>
  select(
    doi_norm, period, publisher, agreement,
    ror_norm, institution_full_name,
    ror_author, institution_display_name,
    author_position, is_corresponding, author_id
  ) |>
  left_join(ror_de, by = c("ror_norm" = "id"), keep = TRUE)
```

```{r}
glimpse(apc_joined)
```

Naming conventions used from here on: 

- `ror_norm` is the ROR ID of the **paying** institution (from OpenAPC), 
- `ror_author` the ROR ID of the **author's affiliation** (from OpenAlex),
- `id` and `relationships` describe the paying institution as recorded in the ROR dataset

### ROR Matching

Checks if the author's affiliation (`ror_author`) matches the paying institution (`ror_norm`) and classifies the match. Only rows with ROR IDs for the paying institution are kept.

Five types of matches are possible and checked in this order:

| `match_type` | meaning | example |
|--------------|---------|---------|
| `exact` | both ROR IDs are identical | University of Regensburg pays, author affiliation is University of Regensburg |
| `author_ror_is_related` | the affiliation is listed as *related* institution in the ROR record of the payer | University of Regensburg pays, author affiliation is University Hospital Regensburg |
| `author_ror_is_child` | the affiliation is listed as *child* (e.g. an institute or faculty) | university pays, author affiliation is one of its institutes |
| `author_ror_is_parent` | the affiliation is listed as *parent* | an institute pays, author affiliation is its university |
| `author_ror_is_predecessor` | the affiliation is listed as *predecessor* | RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau pays, author affiliation is University of Kaiserslautern |
| `NA` | none of the above | university pays, author affiliation is a separate institution |


```{r}
apc_match <- apc_joined |>
  filter(!is.na(ror_norm)) |>
  mutate(
    rel_lower = tolower(relationships),
    parent_list = str_extract(rel_lower, "parent: [^;]*"),
    child_list = str_extract(rel_lower, "child: [^;]*"),
    related_list = str_extract(rel_lower, "related: [^;]*"),
    predecessor_list = str_extract(rel_lower, "predecessor: [^;]*"),
    match_type = case_when(
      ror_norm == ror_author ~ "exact",
      str_detect(parent_list, fixed(ror_author)) ~ "author_ror_is_parent",
      str_detect(child_list, fixed(ror_author)) ~ "author_ror_is_child",
      str_detect(related_list, fixed(ror_author)) ~ "author_ror_is_related",
      str_detect(predecessor_list, fixed(ror_author)) ~ "author_ror_is_predecessor",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    match_exact = match_type %in% "exact"
  )
```

Checking cases that are matched only through ROR relationships.

```{r}
apc_match |>
  filter(!is.na(match_type), !match_exact) |>
  count(institution_full_name, institution_display_name, match_type, sort = TRUE)
```

These are examples of paying institutions and author affiliations where a match could only be established through relationships recorded in the ROR record. The first ten entries show that this is the case for several universities and their university hospitals, because even though these are related institutions they often have separate ROR IDs. Without using ROR relationships these cases would be unmatched.


Checking cases where the ROR record doesn't contain any relationships.

```{r}
apc_match |>
  filter(
    is.na(match_type),
    is.na(relationships)
  ) |>
  count(institution_full_name) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

These are paying institutions where their ROR record doesn't contain any relationships. Thus, for these institutions matching can only succeed through an exact ROR match. This might lead to articles where a match can't be established at all. 


### Categorizing paying institution position

First the aggregated object `article_level` is derived from `apc_match`. `article_level` collapses `apc_match` into one row per DOI. `first()` is used for `period`, `payer_ror`, `payer_name`, `publisher` and `transformative_agreement`, since these are identical across all rows of an article and just need to be carried over once. For the rest, `any()` turns several author rows of an article into one row/answer:

- `has_corr`: is any author marked as corresponding?
- `payer_*`: does the paying institution appear as affiliation of (at least) one author with this position or role? Checks if the payer ROR ID has an exact match or ROR relationship. `payer_any` evaluates if TRUE is returned for any author at all.
- `exact_*`: the same as `payer_*`, but only checks for exact matches.
- `position_category`: the combination of first / middle / last / corresponding. Conditions are checked top to bottom and the first match wins. 


```{r}
article_level <- apc_match |>
  group_by(doi_norm) |>
  summarise(
    period = first(period),
    payer_ror = first(ror_norm),
    payer_name = first(institution_full_name),
    publisher = first(publisher),
    transformative_agreement = any(!is.na(agreement)),
    has_corr = any(is_corresponding %in% TRUE),
    payer_any = any(!is.na(match_type)),
    payer_first = any(!is.na(match_type) & author_position %in% "first"),
    payer_middle = any(!is.na(match_type) & author_position %in% "middle"),
    payer_last = any(!is.na(match_type) & author_position %in% "last"),
    payer_corr = any(!is.na(match_type) & is_corresponding %in% TRUE),
    exact_any = any(match_exact),
    exact_first = any(match_exact & author_position %in% "first"),
    exact_middle = any(match_exact & author_position %in% "middle"),
    exact_last = any(match_exact & author_position %in% "last"),
    exact_corr = any(match_exact & is_corresponding %in% TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(position_category = case_when(
    !payer_any ~ "no match",
    payer_first & payer_last & payer_corr ~ "first + last + corresponding",
    payer_first & payer_corr ~ "first + corresponding",
    payer_last & payer_corr ~ "last + corresponding",
    payer_middle & payer_corr ~ "middle + corresponding",
    payer_first & payer_last ~ "first + last",
    payer_corr ~ "corresponding only",
    payer_first ~ "first only",
    payer_last ~ "last only",
    payer_middle ~ "middle only",
    TRUE ~ "no position match"
  ))
```

```{r}
write_csv(article_level, here("APC_link_analysis/data", "article_level.csv"))
```


Additionally, we precompute two small summary objects:

- `rel_shares`: for each non-exact match type (`related`, `child`, `parent`, `predecessor`), it contains the number and share of distinct articles that were matched through that relationship type. This is used to show how much each relationship type contributes to matching beyond exact ROR ID matches.
- `reason`: for the distinct articles that could not be matched to any author affiliation at all, `reason` shows the number and share attributable to each of the three reasons discussed above (no ROR ID on the affiliation side, no relationships recorded for the payer, or ROR relationships exist but none of them match).


```{r}
only_via_rel_dois <- article_level |>
  filter(payer_any & !exact_any) |>
  pull(doi_norm)

rel_shares <- apc_match |>
  filter(doi_norm %in% only_via_rel_dois, !is.na(match_type)) |>
  group_by(match_type) |>
  summarise(n_articles = n_distinct(doi_norm), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share_of_articles = n_articles / length(only_via_rel_dois))

reason <- apc_match |>
  group_by(doi_norm) |>
  summarise(
    any_match = any(!is.na(match_type)),
    any_affiliation_ror = any(!is.na(ror_author)),
    payer_has_relations = !is.na(first(relationships)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!any_match) |>
  mutate(reason = case_when(
    !any_affiliation_ror ~ "no author affiliation has a ROR ID",
    !payer_has_relations ~ "payer ROR record has no relationships recorded",
    TRUE ~ "ROR exists, but no direct relationship found"
  )) |>
  count(reason) |>
  mutate(
    share_of_no_match = n / sum(n),
    share_of_all_articles = n / n_distinct(apc_match$doi_norm)
  )
```

```{r}
write_csv(rel_shares, here("APC_link_analysis/data", "rel_shares.csv"))
write_csv(reason, here("APC_link_analysis/data", "reason.csv"))
```

## Analysis

### How complete is the coverage of OpenAlex corresponding-author data?

Count and share of corresponding author flags. Shows if at least one author per article is marked as corresponding author.

```{r}
article_level |>
  count(has_corr) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
```

Roughly 92% of articles have at least one author marked as corresponding author in the OpenAlex data. For the other 8%, the policy assumption that APCs are invoiced to the corresponding author's institution can't be tested directly with OpenAlex data alone.


```{r}
article_level |>
  count(has_corr) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = has_corr, y = n, fill = has_corr)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
    vjust = -0.3, size = 3
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.17))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#051740", "FALSE" = "#4086e0"), guide = "none") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "has corresponding author", y = "number of articles")
```


Number of articles and share of corresponding author flags per publication year. Recent years may be less complete.

```{r}
article_level |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    n_articles = n(),
    share_corr_marked = mean(has_corr),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
article_level |>
  count(period, has_corr) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(period), y = n, fill = has_corr)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single", width = 0.9)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
    position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single", width = 0.9),
    vjust = -0.3, size = 3
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.17))) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#051740", "FALSE" = "#4086e0"),
    labels = c("TRUE" = "TRUE", "FALSE" = "FALSE")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "publication year", y = "number of articles", fill = "has \ncorresponding")
```

Coverage is somewhat stable across 2021--2024. For 2025, however, the number of articles are much lower. This is mostly due to a lag in data collection on the OpenAPC end. Institutions submit payment data to OpenAPC which then is normalized and enriched by OpenAPC (see <https://github.com/OpenAPC/openapc-de/wiki/Data-Submission-Handout>). This process takes time, which would explain the lower article count for 2025. Therefore, results for 2025 should be interpreted with caution, and the poster's headline figures are based on the full analysis set rather than a single year.

### How well does ROR-based matching work?

We are especially interested in how many paying institutions and articles can be matched, what ROR relationships add, and where the matching fails (e.g. university hospitals).

Counts and shares of match types per author-affiliation combination.

```{r}
apc_match |>
  count(match_type) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
```

Most author-affiliation combinations show no match at all. This is somewhat expected and might be explained by authors having multiple affiliations and/or co-authored articles where co-authors are not affiliated with the paying institution. Among the author-affiliation combinations that do match, the majority are exact matches.

Counts and shares of distinct paying institutions and articles per match type.

```{r}
apc_match |>
  filter(!is.na(match_type)) |>
  group_by(match_type) |>
  summarise(
    n_payer_rors = n_distinct(ror_norm),
    n_articles = n_distinct(doi_norm),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    share_of_payer_rors = n_payer_rors / n_distinct(apc_match$ror_norm),
    share_of_articles   = n_articles / n_distinct(apc_match$doi_norm)
  )
```

Almost all paying institutions have at least one exact match. However, relying on exact matches only would miss a sizeable share of articles.

Count and shares of distinct articles where the paying institution could be matched to author affiliations via an exact match, only via a relationship, or not at all.

```{r}
article_level |>
  summarise(
    n_articles = n(),
    exact = sum(exact_any),
    only_via_relationships = sum(payer_any & !exact_any),
    no_match = sum(!payer_any),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    share_exact                  = exact / n_articles,
    share_only_via_relationships = only_via_relationships / n_articles,
    share_no_match               = no_match / n_articles
  )
```

Overall, about 87% of articles can be matched exactly. ROR relationships add about an additional 7% of articles to the analysis set which exact ROR ID matching would have missed, leaving about 6% of articles unmatched.

Number of distinct articles where the paying institution could **not** be matched to any author affiliation, differentiated by three reasons: 1) no author affiliation of the article has a ROR ID assigned, 2) at least one author affiliation has a ROR ID, but the ROR record of the paying institution doesn't record any relationships at all, and 3) the paying institution's ROR record does record relationships, but none of them matches any author affiliation of the article. The third reason could either be due to the institutions genuinely not being related, or to how ROR itself organizes relationships. For example, the University of Tübingen is a related organization of the University Hospital of Tübingen, and the University Children's Hospital Tübingen is a child organization of the University Hospital of Tübingen, but there is no direct relationship recorded in ROR between the University of Tübingen and the University Children's Hospital Tübingen.


```{r}
apc_match |>
  group_by(doi_norm) |>
  summarise(
    any_match = any(!is.na(match_type)),
    any_affiliation_ror = any(!is.na(ror_author)),
    payer_has_relations = !is.na(first(relationships)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!any_match) |>
  mutate(reason = case_when(
    !any_affiliation_ror ~ "no author affiliation has a ROR ID",
    !payer_has_relations ~ "payer ROR record has no relationships recorded",
    TRUE ~ "ROR exists, but no direct relationship found"
  )) |>
  count(reason) |>
  mutate(
    share_of_no_match = n / sum(n),
    share_of_all_articles = n / n_distinct(apc_match$doi_norm)
  )
```

For the majority of the unmatched articles the paying institution's ROR record does list relationships, but none of them corresponds to any author affiliation of the article. As illustrated by the Tübingen example above, this does not necessarily mean the institutions are unrelated in practice, but reflects how ROR structures multi-level relationships, which this matching approach, checking only one relationship level, does not fully resolve. A smaller share of unmatched articles is explained by missing ROR IDs on the author-affiliation side, and fewer still by paying institutions whose ROR record has no relationships recorded at all.

### At which author-position is the paying institution recorded as affiliation?

For each article we want to know if the paying institution appears as affiliation of the first, the last, a middle and/or the corresponding author.

The code below shows, separately for articles with and without marked corresponding authors, the share of articles where the paying institution appears as the affiliation of at least one author at each position. Note: position categories are not mutually exclusive, i.e. authors can have a certain position and be marked as corresponding authors at the same time, or several co-authors can be affiliated with the paying institution so that the paying institution appears at different author positions for the same article.


```{r}
article_level |>
  group_by(has_corr) |>
  summarise(
    n_articles      = n(),
    payer_at_first  = mean(payer_first),
    payer_at_last   = mean(payer_last),
    payer_at_middle = mean(payer_middle),
    payer_at_corr   = mean(payer_corr),
    no_match        = mean(!payer_any)
  )
```

For articles without marked corresponding authors, first-author affiliation identifies the paying institution for the large majority of articles. For articles with marked corresponding authors, the paying institution is most comprehensively identified through the corresponding author.

The following code checks the distribution of position categories across publication years.

```{r}
article_level |>
  count(position_category, period) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()
```

The figure below visualizes this distribution, split by whether a corresponding author is marked, with position categories ordered by their maximum share across the two groups.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-align: center

article_level |>
  count(has_corr, position_category) |>
  group_by(has_corr) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(has_corr = factor(has_corr, levels = c(TRUE, FALSE))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = fct_reorder(position_category, share, .fun = max), fill = has_corr)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(
    vars(has_corr),
    labeller = as_labeller(c("TRUE" = "has corresponding-author data", "FALSE" = "has no corresponding-author data"))
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
    hjust = -0.1, size = 5.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#051740", "FALSE" = "#4086e0"), guide = "none") +
  theme_light(base_size = 20) +
  theme(strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#cbd8e8"), strip.text = element_text(colour = "black")) +
  labs(x = "share of articles", y = NULL)
```

For articles with marked corresponding authors, the single largest category is `first + last + corresponding`, meaning the paying institution is simultaneously affiliated with the first author, the last author, and the corresponding author. Combined with the smaller categories that also include *corresponding* (`first + corresponding`, `last + corresponding`, `middle + corresponding`), the paying institution is identified via the corresponding author in the large majority of these articles.

### Are first and/or last author affiliations a good proxy for identifying the paying institution?

We are especially interested in how often the paying institution as first and/or last author affiliation and the paying institution as corresponding author affiliation coincide and what might is missed, if the paying institution is only identified through corresponding-author data.

The code below summarizes, across all articles (not only those with marked corresponding authors), how often the paying institution appears at the corresponding author versus at the first and last author.

```{r}
article_level |>
  summarise(
    n_articles = n(),
    n_payer_at_corresponding = sum(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "first + corresponding",
      "last + corresponding", "middle + corresponding"
    )),
    payer_at_corresponding = mean(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "first + corresponding",
      "last + corresponding", "middle + corresponding"
    )),
    n_payer_at_first = sum(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "first + corresponding",
      "first + last", "first only"
    )),
    payer_at_first = mean(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "first + corresponding",
      "first + last", "first only"
    )),
    n_payer_at_last = sum(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "last + corresponding",
      "first + last", "last only"
    )),
    payer_at_last = mean(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "last + corresponding",
      "first + last", "last only"
    ))
  )
```

Across the full analysis set, the paying institution appears at the first author for a similar share of articles as it appears at the corresponding author, even though corresponding authors are only marked for 92% of articles. This might suggest that first-author affiliation performs comparably to corresponding-author affiliation as an identification strategy. Last author affiliation identifies the paying institution in about 12% less cases than first author affiliation.

Restricting to articles with marked corresponding authors where the paying institution was matched to at least one author at all, the code below checks whether the paying institution matches the first or last author against whether it matches the corresponding author.

```{r}
article_level |>
  filter(has_corr, payer_any) |>
  count(payer_first, payer_last, payer_corr) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
```

First, last and corresponding author agree in the majority of cases. Articles where the corresponding author matches but the first author does not are the cases a first-author proxy would miss. These cases make up for about 8%. Articles where the corresponding author matches but the last author does not are the cases a last-author proxy would miss. These cases make up for about 21%. 

The following checks how much a first-author fallback adds across all articles, i.e. how many additional articles would be captured through the first author affiliation.

```{r}
article_level |>
  summarise(
    corresponding = sum(payer_corr),
    first_additional = sum(payer_first & !payer_corr),
    union_corr_first = sum(payer_corr | payer_first),
    gain_pct = first_additional / union_corr_first
  )
```

Using first-author affiliation as an additional fallback increases the number of identified articles by about 7.1%. This is particularly relevant for the 8% of articles with no marked corresponding authors, where first-author affiliation is an available signal.

We also check how many additional articles would be captured through the last-author affiliation.

```{r}
article_level |>
  summarise(
    corresponding       = sum(payer_corr),
    last_additional     = sum(payer_last & !payer_corr),
    union_corr_last     = sum(payer_corr | payer_last),
    gain_pct            = last_additional / union_corr_last
  )
```

Using last-author affiliation as an additional fallback increases the number of identified articles by about 6.8%, which is a little less than with first-author affiliation.

The Venn diagram below visualizes the overlap between articles where the paying institution matches the corresponding author, articles where it matches the first author, and articles where it matches the last author across the full analysis set.

```{r}
venn_list <- list(
  "Corresponding" = article_level |>
    filter(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "first + corresponding",
      "last + corresponding", "middle + corresponding"
    )) |>
    pull(doi_norm),
  "First" = article_level |>
    filter(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "first + corresponding",
      "first + last", "first only"
    )) |>
    pull(doi_norm),
  "Last" = article_level |>
    filter(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "last + corresponding",
      "first + last", "last only"
    )) |>
    pull(doi_norm)
)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 20
#| fig-height: 14
#| fig-align: center

ggVennDiagram(venn_list, label = "both", set_size = 8, label_size = 8) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#cbd8e8", high = "#051740") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```


The three sets overlap substantially, confirming that first-, last-, and corresponding-author affiliation largely identify the same articles. The areas unique to "First" and/or "Last" represent the practical gain from using first and/or last author as a fallback proxy, while the area unique to "Corresponding" represents articles a first-author-only or last-author-only strategies would miss. However, the combination of "First" and "Last" shows a larger additional gain than the area unique to "Corresponding".
